articles.title: Pakistan: 25 years post-2001
articles.content: THEterrorist eventsof Sept 11, 2001, changed the world and brought about a new security order. Social engineering took place on a large scale, especially within Muslim societies. Conflict erupted across Africa and Asia, often linked to terrorism. These developments triggered large-scale migration towards the West and strengthened the far right in Western societies. Populism took multiple forms. In short, the world changed course, and an era of increasingly controlled societies emerged, affecting technology, the economy, mobility and politics. The 25th anniversary of the tragic incident has triggered a debate: what has the world gained and lost since these events, and what kind of world emerged in their aftermath? This question is equally important for Pakistan, as it became a front-line state in the global war against terrorism. Pakistan’s 25-year experience can perhaps be summarised in one sentence: the country has failed to defeat terrorism completely, lost Afghanistan, witnessed weakened internal cohesion, experienced the rise of authoritarianism, and its economy remains in disarray. Thereturnof the Taliban to power in Afghanistan in 2021 contributed to renewed challenges, particularly from thebanned TTP. Meanwhile, Balochistan remains another major security theatre, with separatist groups targeting security forces, infrastructure, and Chinese interests. Economically, Pakistan received billions of dollars in US assistance and Coalition Support Funds but failed to convert this geopolitical opportunity into lasting economic transformation. Terrorism imposed enormous costs through loss of life, reduced investment, damaged infrastructure, and increased security expenditure. However, Pakistan has also achieved significant strategic successes. Before 9/11, Pakistan was under sanctions because of its nuclear tests. The Kargil conflict had contributed to political instability and military rule, and Pakistan experienced some global isolation. After September 2001, however, Pakistan emerged from isolation to become a front-line ally of the US in its global ‘war on terror’. Pakistan was later designated a major non-Nato ally. However, this partnership came to be characterised by mistrust, particularly over Afghanistan, terrorist sanctuaries, drone strikes, and the 2011 Abbottabad operation. The country’s biggest achievements and major failures have been in counterterrorism. Pakistan’s biggest achievements and major failures have been in counterterrorism. Through operations including Rah-i-Raast, Rah-i-Nijaat,Zarb-i-Azb, and Raddul Fasaad, Pakistan dismantled major terrorist sanctuaries. It ended the ability of terrorist groups to exercise territorial control in areas such as Swat and the former tribal districts. In foreign relations, Pakistan strengthened its strategic partnership with China and expanded ties with the Gulf countries and Türkiye, but its relations with Afghanistan have remained deeply problematic. While it took nearly two decades to fully abandon the use of radical and militant proxies on the external and internal political fronts, two factors played an important role. First, international pressure forced the establishment to take measures against militant groups such as Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed. Second, many members of such groups became disillusioned and joined the TTP, Al Qaeda, and IS-K, making it increasingly difficult for security operators to treat and manage these networks separately. Although these groups are no longer openly active in militancy, they still shoulder political and diplomatic baggage. India frequently exploits this issue to confront Pakistan at the diplomatic level and has used it to build pressure against Pakistan, contributing directly to the military confrontation last year. However, the international community increasingly recognises Pakistan’s efforts to overcome its terrorism problem, and India’s terrorism narrative against Pakistan appears to be losing some of its effectiveness internationally. Over the last 25 years, terrorism has emerged as a core problem for the country, while counterterrorism has become one of its key strengths. Pakistan remains among the countriesmost affected by terrorism. Security concerns have negatively impacted Pakistan-China relations, especially CPEC. At the same time, counterterrorism has provided an avenue for cooperation between the US and Pakistan, and since President Donald Trump took office, the two havedeveloped greater synergyagainst IS-K and in dealing with the Taliban, apart from their multilevel engagement in the Gulf region. In this re-engagement, Pakistan has lost the strategic vision for Afghanistan that Gen Ziaul Haq and his predecessors had crafted. Terrorism and counterterrorism have changed the country’s structure. Counterterrorism has created an imbalance of power, as civilian governments gradually handed over internal and external security affairs to the establishment and refrained from interfering in order to avoid friction. As a result, political engineering became more convenient for the establishment. Social and political engineering have also changed society and left it without direction. Terrorism remains a major obstacle to attracting foreign investment into the country, yet Pakistan’s counterterrorism capabilities have become a strength that allows it to engage with Western and Asian countries. From Gen Pervez Musharraf onwards, military leaders have tried to take credit for the counterterrorism efforts. Yet it is paradoxical that very few acknowledged terrorism as an indigenous problem rooted partly in previous state policies of nurturing militant proxies. In alliance with the clergy, these policies created an infrastructure of extremism in the country. Religious groups were used for multiple purposes — from advancing nationalist projects to acting as pressure groups. Their perception of terrorism was simplistic, and simplistic approaches produced poor policies and flawed strategies. During these years, Pakistan lost 75,366 people, including 3,189 soldiers, 2,598 FC personnel, 3,599 police officers, and 26,547 civilians, apart from casualties in other security institutions. Pakistan launched 2,961 military operations, both medium- and large-scale, against terrorists, in addition to several other types of military operations against terrorism. The country has established dedicated counterterrorism institutions, including Nacta (lately in the news for another reason), counter-extremism centres, NFTIC, and others. Pakistan has also produced 13 policy documents, ranging from the National Action Plan and National Security Policy to Paigham-i-Pakistan. After all these sacrifices, operations, institutions, and policy documents, is Pakistan still searching for a new counterterrorism policy?
articles.author: Muhammad Amir Rana

articles.title: Britain’s liberal establishment
articles.content: THE opera Die Entführung aus dem Serail (The Abduction from the Seraglio) by Mozart composed in 1782, was superbly produced at Glyndebourne this summer. One reviewer noted that, since the opera embodies the late 18th-century fascination with “all things Oriental”, the director sets it in the period of its composition, “largely discounting historical anachronisms and showing less interest in cultural value judgements”. This remark is revealing of how British conservative — with a small ‘c’ — intellectuals view what they describe as the hegemony of liberals across public spheres and institutions, labelling them the ‘liberal British establishment’. For them, political correctness has gone too far; conformity with liberal values is ‘woke’. Pakistani intellectuals tend to socialise largely with their liberal-left British peers. The terms ‘liberal elite’ and ‘cosmopolitan elite’ increasingly serve as metaphors for groups that have prospered from globalisation, the European Union project, and the post-Second World War global liberal order. Brexit and the rise of the far-right Reform Party have epitomised resentment towards this established ‘liberal’ political class. Institutions such as the BBC, elite universities including Oxford and Cambridge, and even the British civil service are often perceived as standard-bearers of the domestic liberal establishment. One also encounters claims that PhD humanities funding for work on straight, white men has become harder to secure; that young academics researching conservative themes face limited prospects because of liberal-left dominance in academia. Criticising liberal cultural values as ‘woke’ whilst divorcing them from the economic consequences of neoliberalism offers no answers. Conservative critics see ‘woke’ culture as a pendulum that has swung too far. There is also an argument that Britain has failed the white working class. This was reflected in the fall of the so-called Labour Party ‘Red Wall’ in the formerly industrial British Midlands, as sections of the white working class deserted Labour for Reform in recent local elections. The Conservatives have also lost heavily to Reform. Far-right parties such as Reform, however, offer few solutions to the real economic causes of this political rupture. Instead, they capitalise on working-class grievances, galvanising support around issues such as migration. The white working class lagging behind is perhaps the only valid strand of the far-right argument. This is because the proverbial trickle-down effect of the neoliberal economic model did not reach the working classes, regardless of race, resulting in the unevenly distributed proceeds of economic growth. Margaret Thatcher, portrayed as an apostle of neoliberalism, was convinced that Milton Friedman’s monetarism was a “scientific doctrine”. Yet in 2003, Friedman himself admitted to the Financial Times that “the use of quantity of money as a target has not been a success”. Neoliberals failed to fulfil their promise that working classes would catch up after the initial inequalities, a claim that is central to the idea of economic progress under capitalism. Yet neoliberalism survived the 2008 Great Financial Crisis. Conservative prime minister Liz Truss was punished by financial markets for her unfunded tax cuts in 2022. Andy Burnham became prime minister promising to address regional inequalities, but he had to calm the bond markets even before entering parliament after his previous statement that “this country should not be in hock to the bond markets” sent jitters through the markets. In the US, the rise of Zohran Mamdani, the New York mayor, and President Donald Trump reflects a similar disconnect between cosmopolitans and the country. While Mamdani’s victory is celebrated by liberals and progressives, they need to reckon with the fact that it is also a symptom of the widening gulf. Academics and public intellectuals are trying to grapple with the rise of right-wing populism, particularly in the West. Some draw analogies with Europe’s mid-14th-century social and political crises, in the aftermath of Black Death, the Hundred Years’ War between England and France, and peasant revolts in both countries. Other writers draw on Hugh Trevor-Roper’s 1959 essay, The General Crisis of the 17th Century. As Alan Wooldridge argues, Brexit Britain resembles Oliver Cromwell’s Roundhead Britain: small towns and the countryside resenting elite institutions. Contemporary populists rail against elites much as Cromwell and his supporters opposed the court, believing that elites embrace global rather than national values. Anglo-Catholicism was once a marker of sophistication, while university degrees serve a similar function today to court connections in the 17th century. Some draw parallels with 1930s populism, which contributed to the rise of Hitler and Mussolini, and was fomented by the economic crisis that ensued from the Great Depression of 1929. But the problem with neoliberalism is deeper. Criticising liberal cultural values as ‘woke’ whilst divorcing them from the economic consequences of neoliberalism offers no answers; it merely reinforces the far-right narrative against ‘woke’ culture. The attack on liberalism and the Enlightenment project has been mounted by postmodernists, structuralists and poststructuralists, conservatives, socialists, nationalists, multiculturalists, communitarians and even libertarians, who share ancestry with classical liberalism. While historical populism analogies and critiques of liberalism may have merit, revisiting liberalism’s evolution over the past two centuries may better explain today’s political rupture. As I previously wrote in these pages, the rise of a mass working class during the late 19th and early 20th centuries — a product of the Industrial Revolution — brought profound socioeconomic shifts and heightened inequality. Modern liberals recognised that classical principles of mere physical freedom were no longer sufficient. They began advocating state-provided social welfare to enable individuals to realise their potential — a modern understanding of ‘freedom’. Figures such as John Stuart Mill can be seen as transitional figures bridging classical liberalism and modern social liberalism. Neoliberals would do well to revisit how earlier liberals embraced social welfare in response to rising inequality. The English upper classes who gather at the opera may have a point: centuries-old traditions deserve to be preserved and experienced within the cultural worlds that gave them meaning. Yet they must also confront an uncomfortable irony — that they have prospered from economic liberalism, and that liberalism, taken as a whole, carries cultural values that may strike its conservative critics as distinctly ‘woke’. The writer teaches economics at SOAS, University of London, and is associated with Bloomsbury Pakistan.
articles.author: Nadir Cheema

articles.title: Promises on stage
articles.content: ON Tuesday before the anniversary, on the lawns of the White House, the president of the United States told a story about two firemen. They were big men, he said. Donald Trump is not a small man himself. The building beside them had started to creak and they thought it was coming down on top of them. So they grabbed Trump under the arms, lifted him off the ground and whisked him away. He told them he could run himself. They kept going. The occasion was an event honouring the emergency responders of Sept 11, three days before the 25th anniversary of 9/11. He has told the tale before at a campaign stop in New Hampshire in 2016. What is worth noticing is not the story. It is the direction in which it has been travelling. On the day itself, Trump gave a phone interview to a local station and said he had spoken to someone who saw at least 10 people jump. Two days later, he was near the site, talking to reporters. He had 100 men down there, he said, and another 125 on the way. He was there to spur them on. That is the earliest version. A man who sent workers. By November 2015, at a rally in Columbus, he had watched people jump himself — from a window in his apartment four miles uptown. You cannot see a person at four miles. By April 2016, in Buffalo, he said he had helped clear the rubble. A little bit, he said. And now — he was being lifted off the ground by firemen who feared for his life. Commemoration in Pakistan is an occasion for announcements. Twenty-five years, and he has moved from the edge of the frame to the middle of it. He has since written on Truth Social that he was not there on the day of the collapse but shortly afterwards. The correction never travels as far as the story. Notice where these versions were delivered. Columbus, a rally. Birmingham, a rally, where he also said thousands had cheered in Jersey City as the towers fell, which the police there had already denied. Buffalo, a rally. New Hampshire, a campaign stop. The White House lawn last week. The story grows in front of audiences. On Friday, he was at the Pentagon. He had wanted to be in New York then changed the plan once it was clear he would not be allowed to speak. The ceremony there has barred politicians from speaking since 2012. It is hours of families reading names aloud. There is nothing to announce, and it offers a president nothing. Our societies are built the other way around. Every commemoration we have has a dais, a chief guest and a running order. The families are seated. Someone speaks. This is not a failure of etiquette. It is the design. A Pakistani commemoration is not an occasion for remembering. It is an occasion for announcing. And what gets announced is a promise. Compensation. An inquiry. A committee. A resolve that this will never happen again. The promise is the reason the stage is there, because a promise is a thing only the powerful can make, and it has to be made in front of the people it is being made to. In December 2014, gunmen walked into the Army Public School in Peshawar and killed 132 children. In my lifetime, I thought it was the closest this country has come to a moment when everything might have stopped. I remember thinking, this is it. There is no argument left. Someone will have to fix the thing itself now. What the country produced was a plan. Twenty points. Military courts. A National Action Plan, which is an honest name, because the action was the plan. Here is the part I keep returning to. It did not quietly expire. In June 2024, the multi-domain Azm-i-Istehkam campaign was launched, and the National Action Plan was there to justify it. What was announced beside the coffins of children in 2014 was still working in 2024. Catastrophe here does not produce repair. It produces structure. The school is not made safe. A framework is built. The framework outlasts the grief that authorised it, and it can be pointed later at whatever needs pointing at. Now we are discussing new provinces. The conversation has arrived, as these conversations do, after something didn’t quite work out the way we thought and it is being offered as an answer to it. Redraw the map. Change the units. New assemblies, new seats, a new tier of government. I am not going to argue here about whether new provinces are a good idea. Ask the smaller question. In 10 years, when something terrible happens again and the stage goes up and someone stands at it, what will they be holding? What did these debates leave behind, and who will it be used against? We keep waiting for the incident that finally ends the argument. It does not come. There is no version of this where the grief is large enough. The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: Terrible 9/11
articles.content: THE 11th day of September, 2001 (9/11), started out as an ordinary day in bustling New York. As residents headed to work, the first planestruck one of the twin towersof the World Trade Centre at 8.46 am. Minutes later, another plane hit the second one. A third plane hit the Pentagon building while a fourth was downed in Pennsylvania. This was a massive terrorist attack against what was then the world’s sole superpower. An ordinary day had turned into a watershed moment for global geopolitics. So much changed so rapidly. First, transnational terrorism emerged on top of the global priority list. Prompted by the US, the UN Security Council adopted on Sept 28, 2001, Resolution 1373, which bound all member states to prevent, suppress, and criminalise the financing of terrorism. A few years later, Resolution 1540 was adopted by the UNSC, obliging member states to prevent non-state actors from acquiring weapons of mass destruction. Thus evolved a comprehensive global ecosystem against non-state actors carrying out terrorist attacks anywhere in the world. Second, the US and Nato countries launched a ferocious attack against Taliban-led Afghanistan, which had given refuge to Al Qaeda, the group the US held responsible for 9/11. This embroiled Washington in awarthat became its longest since the end of World War II. With Pakistan’s help, the US was able to eliminate the Al Qaeda leadership, except for Osama bin Laden, who was killed later in 2011. However, the US war against the Taliban dragged on with no success. The US tried to blame Pakistan for its military defeat in Afghanistan because of the support that the Taliban had allegedly received. Pakistan’s view all along was that this issue should be resolved via political means. The US later took Pakistan’s advice and concluded a peace deal with the Taliban in February 2020, but did not take the second piece of advice regarding a responsible withdrawal. Instead, it abruptly withdrew its troops from Afghanistan in August 2021, creating a vacuum that was filled by the Taliban rather than an interim government comprising all Afghan factions. Further, the US left behind massive arms and ammunition, which have since been used for terrorism by entities like the TTP and BLA. Sadly, 25 years after 9/11, Afghanistan is once again a sanctuary for global terrorists. Third, barely two years after 9/11, the US decided to invade Iraq to destroy alleged weapons of mass destruction. This attack set a dangerous precedent of using force illegally (not sanctioned by the UNSC) and pre-emptively, ie, merely on suspicion. This precedent has since been followed by other powers against their adversaries, as seen in the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2014 and 2022 and India’s aggression against Pakistan in 2016, 2019, and 2025. Armed conflicts have now expanded to every corner of the world. According to the ICRC, there are 130 active armed conflicts worldwide. The events of 9/11 changed so much so rapidly. Fourth, Pakistan became the front-line state in the US-led global war against terrorism, mainly because America needed Pakistan’s help in fighting Al Qaeda based in neighbouring Afghanistan. Pakistan ended up not only having to deal with infiltrating terrorists and extremists from Afghanistan but also prosecuting extremist outfits that had taken root in the country ever since the days of the so-called Afghan jihad of the 1980s. Pakistan thus found itself “in the line of fire” — the title of Gen Musharraf’s book. Fifth, the events of 9/11 provided India a self-serving opportunity to team up with the West against so-called radical Islam and project itself as a victim of what New Delhi alleged was Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in Indian-occupied Kashmir. India also used the occasion to cast the Kashmiri struggle for the right to self-determination as transnational terrorism. Sixth, the new concept ‘responsibility to protect’ was born, with powerful countries arguing that if a state’s leadership was unable or unwilling to protect its own people, then it became the responsibility of the international community to protect them. Using this concept, the West intervened in several Arab countries to bring about regime change. This was described as‘Arab Spring’, but, as time showed, the events destabilised the entire Middle East and turned out to be an ‘Arab autumn’. The terrorist incidents of 9/11 profoundly changed global and regional geopolitics. The era of globalisation became the first casualty. The use of force emerged as the main arbiter of international disputes. The definition between freedom struggle and terrorism was blurred. Multilateralism was marginalised and international law violated with impunity. The world disorder that one sees today is rooted in what happened on 9/11 — that fateful September day. The writer is chairman Sanober Institute and former foreign secretary of Pakistan.
articles.author: Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry

articles.title: Iran war endgame
articles.content: US PRESIDENT Donald Trump haspredictedthat the Iran war will end “very soon”. Yet the facts on the ground belie this assumption. While speaking in Ireland on Saturday, the American leader repeated that in his calculation, the conflict would wind down “right after election time”, referring to US midterm polls in November. However, much can happen between now and November, and wars are not cut-and-dry affairs that can be ended with the push of a button. If he is serious about concluding the war, Mr Trump should immediately reach out to the Iranians to achieve a negotiated solution. After all, there is much to worry about as the war — and its connected conflicts — have spread across the Middle East. There have been intermittent exchanges between the US and Iran over the past few days. Meanwhile, the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire hascollapsed, with the pro-Iran group seizing more territory in Yemen, and aiming its guns at the Bab al-Mandeb strait to prevent Saudi vessels from crossing it. On the other hand, the East-West oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia — a critical alternative for transporting petroleum after the Hormuz blockade — has beenstruckapparently from Iraq. Riyadh has said it has held off on taking action after a request from the “brotherly Iraqi government” but reserves the right to respond. Though powerful pro-Iran militias are active in Iraq, no group had, at the time of writing, taken responsibility for the attack. In Lebanon, Israel continues its savage bombardment as it tries to bring Hezbollah to its knees. Thousands of Lebanese have been killed in these brutal attacks, while hundreds of thousands have been displaced. It should be remembered that a ceasefire in Lebanon was a crucial part of the Islamabad MoU. All these interconnected conflicts indicate that a Middle East ceasefire cannot wait for November. As the aggressor in this war, the US should take the first step by ending hostilities with Iran; Tehran should respond in kind.Talksbetween Iran and the Gulf states regarding the Strait of Hormuz are scheduled in Oman on Monday. Hopefully, the regional states can reach an agreement for the reopening of the crucial waterway. As a confidence-building measure, the US should announce the cessation of hostilities against Iran, and an end to the blockade of Iranian ports. Wars are unpredictable, and American confidence that Washington can control the tempo of hostilities till November is misplaced. A peaceful solution is required now. Moreover, the war is deeply unpopular in the US, and many top American generals have reportedly warned their bosses against escalating. Therefore, it is time to end this futile misadventure, and reopen channels of dialogue through trusted third parties such as Pakistan and other regional states.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Smog response
articles.content: PUNJAB’S decision to begin fighting smog before the air turns poisonous deserves support. For years, the province’s response to winter pollution has too often appeared reactive: schools close, outdoor activity is restricted and emergency measures follow once Lahore’s air becomes hazardous. The latest “pre-smog crackdown”, targeting construction dust, dry sweeping, crop-residue and waste burning, brick kilns, and vehicle emissions, is therefore a sensible change in approach. Some of the new steps are practical: ending dry sweeping, requiring wet or mechanical cleaning, covering construction material, checking vehicle emissions and using technology to identify violations can reduce avoidable pollution. Making dust-control compliance at construction sites a condition of project approval would be useful, provided penalties apply equally to public and private projects. Likewise, farmers should be helped to dispose of crop residue through modern machinery rather than simply punished for burning it; enforcement without affordable alternatives will invite evasion. The real test, however, is implementation. Punjab already has rules against waste burning, emissions standards and dust-control protocols, yet the EPA itself says inspections in Lahore found poor compliance at several development projects despite SOPs issued last year. That should temper official claims of progress. Punjab must resist treating smog as a three-month problem. Transport, industry, waste management and urban construction pollute throughout the year. Winter weather merely traps these emissions closer to the ground and makes the consequences harder to ignore. Cleaner public transport, stricter vehicle fitness regimes, better fuel quality, modernised industry, proper waste collection and continuous air-quality monitoring matter as much as raids and fines. Authorities should publish emissions data, inspection results and penalties so the public can judge whether enforcement is sustained and whether repeat offenders are being deterred. Greater coordination among provincial departments and city authorities is important. Citizens, too, have a role, but official appeals for cooperation cannot replace governance. Individuals cannot regulate kilns, redesign transport systems or police construction sites. Those are state responsibilities. Punjab is right to act before October, but the crackdown will only count as progress if it becomes routine.
articles.author: Editorial
